responses.id: ART-0007/Initial assessment and why it was wrong
responses.text: The first assessment pointed upstream, to an interruption in the overnight window. On the evidence available at the time that was the reasonable read: the failure appeared in an overnight batch, the job had no history of reference-data faults, and an upstream interruption would have produced precisely the symptom seen. It was tested rather than assumed, and it did not survive the test — {{fact:FACT-0005}}. That finding is what redirected the investigation from infrastructure to data, and it did so within the same working day. Recording the hypothesis was not the error, and this section should not be read as though it were. Withholding an assessment until it was certain would have left the incident without a working direction during exactly the hours when the close was most at risk. The hypothesis did its job by being specific enough to disprove quickly.

claims.text: Log evidence ruled out an interruption during the valuation window.

responses.text: The confirmed cause is {{fact:FACT-0006}}. The initial assessment, {{fact:FACT-0004}}, was set aside when {{fact:FACT-0005}}. What allowed that mapping to reach production stale is a separate question from what broke, and it is the more important one. The mapping between the legacy and current category structures has been maintained by hand since the remap rather than migrated into the merchandising master, so it drifts whenever the structure moves and nothing reconciles it back. The classification recorded against this incident is {{fact:FACT-0013}}. The ownership position is the finding: {{fact:FACT-0014}}. An unowned control is not a control. There is no team that would have been expected to notice the drift, no reviewer whose sign-off was skipped, and therefore no process failure to point at — which is precisely why this recurred rather than being caught. Treating the stale mapping as the cause and stopping there would leave the condition that produced it entirely intact.

responses.text: The period's inventory valuation did not complete. The feed reported {{fact:FACT-0002}}, stopping the run outright rather than degrading it, so the failure surfaced at once instead of as a discrepancy found weeks later. The scope was {{fact:FACT-0007}} — a large enough share of the catalogue that no partial valuation would have been defensible. The consequence fell on the timetable rather than on any reported figure: valuation had to be completed by other means before the ledger could be locked, and nothing downstream of it could proceed until it was. Anyone reading only this section should take away three things. The run failed cleanly and visibly rather than silently. Its scope was material. And the mechanism behind it is one this organisation has been carrying deliberately since the category structure was remapped, which is why the sections below spend more time on the condition than on the fault.

responses.text: Confirm the valuation run has stopped rather than merely slowed; check job status before changing anything. Identify the unresolved hierarchy nodes from the run log and record them on the incident — that list is what any eventual fix needs. Apply the override: {{fact:FACT-0009}}. Re-run valuation for the period and confirm it completes end to end rather than resuming from the failure point. Reconcile the valued total against the prior period before releasing it; a mapping override that silently drops items will still complete. Attach both the override applied and the node list to the incident record. Finally, raise or update the ownership ticket. Do not close the incident on a successful re-run alone — the run completing means the period is recoverable, not that the fault is gone.
